name: Wistman's Wood

location.address: West Dart valley, north of Two Bridges, Dartmoor National Park, Devon

official_register.name: Natural England SSSI record (Wistman's Wood, notified 1964)

access: National Nature Reserve on open moor, free; Natural England and the Dartmoor National Park Authority ask visitors to follow the paths around the wood and not to enter it (erosion damages the lichens and mosses). View from the path at the edge. Roughly a 25 minute walk north from the Two Bridges car park on the B3357.
transport: Two Bridges on the B3357 (car park opposite the Two Bridges Hotel); public bus not verified.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a low, mossy wood of twisted oaks among granite boulders on the hillside above the West Dart. It is about a 25 minute walk north of the Two Bridges car park, seen from the path along its edge.
verify_notes: Ensemble as the destination: one wood, one place to stand outside it. Wikipedia: 3.5 ha in North, Middle and South Groves, 380 to 410 m altitude; most oaks rarely exceed 4.5 m, a few 6 to 7.6 m, in 1997 maximum about 12 m and average about 7 m; oldest oaks appear 400 to 500 years; an oak felled in 1866 was about 168 years old. SSSI notified 1964; NNR; about 120 lichen species; owned by the Duchy of Cornwall, managed under a nature reserve agreement since 1961; 2023 plan with Natural England to reduce grazing and foot traffic and expand the rainforest by 2040 (Guardian, 3 Jul 2023). Described c. 1620 as oaks no taller than a man could touch the top of with his head. Species conflict: Wikipedia says mainly pedunculate oak with some rowan; Countryfile says sessile oak; used pedunculate per Wikipedia, check the Natural England citation. Countryfile's '6,000 years old' wood claim not used. Pin is the Wikipedia coordinate for the wood (grid ref SX612774 vs SX612772 in the same article), approximate; the viewing point on the public path was not separately fixed, so the writer must not claim a viewing coordinate. Two Bridges Hotel states no access restriction, the official bodies ask people not to enter: access line follows the official request. Alive: lifecheck RECENT 2026-05-13 (iNaturalist 361227592 at the coordinate). Photos not hunted (Commons/Geograph will have plenty). Writing pass 2026-11-04: lead photo Geograph 7090655 (Ian Capper, 2022) approved. Species kept as pedunculate: Wikipedia and a published oakwood study (archive.org biostor-129949) name Quercus robur; Countryfile's sessile is the outlier; the Natural England citation PDF was not retrievable.
story:
Around 1620 a visitor described the oaks of Wistman's Wood as no taller than a man could reach the top of with his head. Four centuries later most of them still rarely pass 4.5 metres. They grow at 380 to 410 metres up on the open moor above the West Dart, rooted among granite boulders, low, twisted and thick with moss.

This is a wood, not a tree, and the wood is the destination. It covers about 3.5 hectares in three groves, North, Middle and South. The oldest oaks appear to be 400 to 500 years old; one felled in 1866 turned out to be about 168. Wikipedia names them mainly pedunculate oak with some rowan, while one walking guide says sessile, so the exact species is less settled than the place.

What the boulders hold is the treasure. About 120 species of lichen grow here, and erosion from feet does real damage to them and to the mosses. That is why Natural England and the national park ask visitors to stay on the paths around the edge and not to go in. The view from the path is the visit.

The wood has been a Site of Special Scientific Interest since 1964 and is owned by the Duchy of Cornwall. A plan agreed in 2023 aims to cut grazing and foot traffic and let this rainforest spread by 2040.

name: Meavy Oak
age_estimate: said to be 800 to nearly 1,000 years

location.address: Village green outside the Royal Oak Inn, in front of St Peter's churchyard wall, Meavy, Devon

access: Village green, public, free; Burrator Parish Council owns the green. Beside a pub and cars park nearby.
transport: Meavy village on the south-west edge of Dartmoor, west of Burrator Reservoir; bus not verified.
how_to_recognise: The hollow ancient oak on the green between the Royal Oak pub and the churchyard wall, propped by supports.
verify_notes: ALIVE UNCONFIRMED: lifecheck NONE. Tavistock Today 15 Feb 2019: arboricultural report described the tree as in irreversible decline, a very advanced state of decline, at risk of collapse, with a quarter of the trunk still feeding the canopy (per Escape to Britain, search snippet only); urgent pruning planned before mid-March 2019 to keep it standing. Burrator Parish Council 2023 minutes mention 150 to 200 saplings grown from its acorns as possible successors (search snippet); July 2024 agenda and 27 Mar 2025 minutes mention a survey of the oaks on Meavy Green (snippet; unclear whether this is the Royal Oak). No 2025 or 2026 sighting found: a session must confirm it still stands before it ships. Age: believed nearly 1,000 years (Tavistock Today 2017/2019), over 900 per Wikipedia, over 800 per Dartmoor Links, over 950 per Dartmoor NPA veteran-trees page (snippet); legend ties it to King John's reign, folklore. Described by Loudon in Arboretum (1838) (Wikipedia). Folklore girth 26 ft hollow enough for 9 diners (Dartmoor Trust record, snippet), no measured girth found. Wikipedia lists the oak photo on Commons from Geograph. Shortlisted for Woodland Trust National Tree of the Year (Tavistock Today 21 Sep 2017). Coordinate is the Wikipedia village centre, not the tree. Writing pass 2026-11-04: held. No dated 2024 or later sighting found (Geograph search: latest photos naming the oak 2006 and 2015; substack post 2023 behind a paywall; 2025 fair listing and parish agendas do not show it).
hold: no evidence it stands after 2019: a 2019 arboricultural report found it in irreversible decline and at risk of collapse; no dated 2024 or later sighting or photograph found (Geograph's latest named photo of the oak is 2015; a 2025 Meavy Oak Fair listing and 2023 to 2025 parish papers do not show the tree alive)
